newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: New KLM boss seen as frank pragmatist.
newsitem.headline: New KLM boss seen as frank pragmatist.

text.p: Officially, Leo van Wijk only takes over as boss of Dutch airline KLM on Tuesday, but industry sources say he has already pulled off his first major success.

Van Wijk, 50, is widely credited with engineering last week's much-needed reconciliation with KLM's U.S. partner Northwest Airlines, ending a protracted boardroom battle which had blocked further development of their lucrative alliance.
The accord on a renewable 10-year operational agreement in return for KLM's 19 percent voting stake in Northwest bears all the hallmarks of Van Wijk's pragmatic approach, analysts say.
"It was Van Wijk who conducted the talks with Northwest in recent months and it was his commercial insight that swung the deal," said one analyst who declined to be named.
"I have the impression that (outgoing KLM president Pieter) Bouw had become too rigid in his attitudes...it needed Van Wijk to come along and add some water to the wine," he said.

After a string of acrimonious run-ins with Northwest directors over KLM's option to up its 19 percent Northwest voting stake by another five percent in 1998, Bouw increasingly left the Northwest negotiations to his chief operating officer.
"Over the years I think the dispute with Northwest escalated into a clash of personalities," said one industry source.
"Van Wijk was able to stand back from all that...he is certainly more pragmatic than Bouw and not as concerned to protect the KLM identity at all costs."
While Bouw won a reputation as a thinker and a visionary, Van Wijk is seen as more of a doer and a decison-maker.
"Bouw had some good ideas -- he was the pioneer behind the global network concept," said an insider who refused to be named. "But he was no diplomat."
By contrast Van Wijk is an accomplished negotiator, respected by unions and investors alike for his straight-talking pragmatism and willingness to compromise.
"He's done very well on the Northwest deal -- a 10-year operating contract is quite an achievement when five years might have done as well," said an analyst.
Another notes Van Wijk's good contacts with labour unions, reflected in the recent pay-and-conditions accord reached with pilots.

A true-blue "career KLM-er" who has worked for the airline all his life since graduating from the University of Amsterdam with a degree in econometrics in 1971, Van Wijk will need to capitalise on his assets in the years ahead.

Most analysts agree that costs at the airline -- particularly staff costs -- are still rising too fast, while the majority of measures proposed under KLM's ambitious Focus 2000 programme to reduce overheads and boost operating revenues have yet to be implemented.

Given last week's announcement by the largest Dutch trade union federation FNV that it plans to abandon wage moderation in upcoming pay-and-conditions talks for 1998, it looks like Van Wijk has a busy time ahead.

On a more positive note, however, the deal with Northwest will facilitate KLM's search for a new ally to strengthen its European network and build up market share. Prime candidates for a Euro-alliance have been named as Alitalia and, to a lesser degree, Swissair, though the latter's link with U.S. Delta Airlines could prove a stumbling block. -- Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000
